content.thinking:
This looks like a monitoring gap rather than a real outage—error rates actually improved and logs kept flowing past 21:10, meaning the logging pipeline was fine but the metrics scrape broke. I need to write this up carefully, making clear that the "broken for 0.12 hours" figure refers specifically to the metrics absence, not to any user-facing impact.

My assumptions: the 21:11 deployment caused this, confirmed by the rollback restoring metrics; the scrape likely keys on port name; continued normal service is inferred from logs alone since metrics can't confirm impact during the gap; and the rollback is validated by metrics returning to baseline rather than by directly verifying user impact was fixed. I'll frame the executive summary generically as "the shop's monitoring" rather than naming specific tools like Prometheus.

assumptions: That io-shop kept serving traffic normally during the gap is inferred from its application logs, not measured - while metrics were absent there was by definition no metric data for that window, so no service-health figure for those minutes can be treated as observed.

The published before/during error-rate figures are not evidence of an improvement or of impact; the 'during' numbers come from a window in which io-shop's own metrics were missing, and the small negative rise above baseline is an artifact of that, not a real effect of the change.

The incident duration is a lower bound: metrics were still absent at the last minute of data read, and the true end of the visibility gap is taken to be when reporting returned at 21:18 after the rollback.

Causation is attributed to the 21:11 deployment on the strength of the timing and the fact that rollback restored metrics; the scrape configuration itself was not inspected directly to prove the selector keys on the port name.
The flag provider showed no recent changes, so feature flags were ruled out rather than investigated further.

The alternative framing the investigator considered - treating the scrape/service-monitor configuration as deployed application config rather than part of the monitoring pipeline - was never tested; it describes the same portName rename and does not change the remediation.
input.executive_summary: Starting at 21:11 UTC on 2026-09-30, we lost visibility into one of the shop's services: it stopped reporting the health data we monitor it with. A configuration change shipped in a routine release renamed an internal label that our monitoring uses to find the service, so the monitoring simply no longer knew where to look. The service itself continued to serve shoppers normally the whole time — its own activity logs kept flowing and showed account pages rendering with only the same low level of routine "shopper closed the page" errors seen before the change. So there is no evidence of customer-visible impact; the incident was a blind spot in our ability to observe the service rather than an outage of it. The alert fired at 21:16 UTC, an automated responder picked it up within seconds, identified the release as the likely cause, and reverted it. Reporting returned to normal at 21:18 UTC, roughly seven minutes after the visibility gap began. No code defect was found, so no follow-up code change was made; the fix was to undo the release.
input.root_cause: A deployment of io-shop at 21:11:00Z renamed the Prometheus scrape port in the service's production values from `metrics` to `http-metrics`. The scrape target selector keys on that port name, so the moment the new revision came up the target stopped matching and metrics collection for io-shop ceased; the application itself was untouched and, per its logs, kept serving account-page traffic throughout. Rolling back to the previous revision restored the port name and metrics resumed, which confirmed the cause.
